headline: Why Are the Sod Bank Fluke Suddenly Ignoring Your Bucktail?
subhead: Warm water has made Absecon and Great Egg's fluke lazy and choosy — here's why bigger baits are outfishing the standard strip-and-bucktail rig this week.
body_markdown:
I got the same question three times at the dock this week, so let's make it a lesson: why is a five-inch Gulp strip on a half-ounce bucktail — the rig that's caught fluke in these back bays for thirty summers — suddenly getting refused? The short answer is water temperature. The long answer is worth understanding if you want to keep filling the cooler through Labor Day.

All that rain we've taken over the last three-plus weeks — eight-plus inches of it — has pushed a lot of tannic, off-color water into the marsh creeks and stained the shallow flats behind Ocean City and Sea Isle. Fluke don't love hunting hard in dirty, warm water. What they'll do instead is park on a piece of structure — a bulkhead corner, a channel edge, a bridge piling — and wait for something to come to them. That's a fish conserving energy, not one chasing bait. So this week the program that's actually working is bigger, not flashier: whole squid strips, bluefish belly strips cut long, or a Gulp Swimming Mullet in white threaded onto a full ounce of lead, fished dead slow right on bottom in the deeper holes of the Absecon Channel and the sod bank drop-offs off Brigantine. Slow-rolled, almost stalled, tight to structure — that's the difference between three keepers and none this week. I had a mixed bag of fluke to 19 inches doing exactly this off the Rainbow Channel bend on the last two hours of the outgoing, when that cooler ocean water is still pushing through and the fish set up right on the seam.

Great Egg Inlet is fishing the same way — the fluke are there, they're just concentrated tight to the inlet mouth where tidal flow keeps the water a few degrees cooler than the stagnant flats up in the back. If you're marking bait on the meter around the Rt. 52 causeway rock piles, drop straight down with a heavier bucktail than you think you need. I wasted two hours last Tuesday guessing wrong on weight before I finally got bit.

Bluefish are the one thing in this bay you can set your watch by right now, and we called this a week ago — said the snapper blues packing the back bays would keep building toward adult class fish, and that's exactly what's happening. Absecon Inlet and the mouth of the Mullica have snappers thick enough to chum with sand, but mixed in now are real 3- to 4-pound choppers, with the occasional fish pushing 6 or 7. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — worked fast through the froth at first light is the play, before the sun gets high and pushes them down. If you're throwing bait, cut bunker chunks fished under a float in the rips at Great Egg on the outgoing will keep you busy without needing to cast a rod.

Striped bass, I'll be honest with you, are a tough sell right now. Bay water in the high 70s to 80 degrees shuts bass down to a narrow window — I'm talking the hour before and after first light, working current seams at the Absecon Inlet rock jetty or the Route 30 bridge pilings with a Storm 360GT Searchbait swimbait or a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig. You might get two or three bites in that window and then it's dead until the sun drops again. Don't plan a whole trip around them yet — plan a trip that has bass as the bonus if you're out early for blues or fluke anyway.

Kingfish are quietly one of the better bets on this beat right now if you don't mind standing in the wash. Ocean City and Stone Harbor surf, first and second bar, bloodworms or Fishbites on a high-low bottom rig, has been steady for kingfish in the 8- to 11-inch range with the occasional bonus weakfish mixed in on the same rig — though I want to be straight with you, weakfish numbers are thin this year, a fish here and there working the deeper Great Egg channel edges on a dropping tide, nothing you should plan a trip around. Triggerfish have started showing on the rock piles inside Absecon Inlet, a genuine late-summer visitor when the water holds warm this long — small pieces of clam or shrimp fished tight to the rocks on light tackle will find them, and they're a fun change of pace even if they're not going in anyone's cooler.

Looking ahead, tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should push more water and more bait through these inlets and tighten up the fluke bite on structure even further — that's usually when the bigger doormats start showing on the same drop-offs that are holding shorts now. If the rain holds off and that stained water clears out of the back bays even a little, I'd expect the fluke to get more aggressive again and go back to eating a standard strip-and-bucktail. Until then, go bigger, go slower, and fish the seams where clean water meets dirty. That's the lesson this week, and it's one worth remembering every time we get a soaked August like this one.
